notes: Species templates (real organisms or groups). firstAge/lastAge are GeologicalAge names; empty lastAge = still alive today. Sizes are typical adult body lengths.

species.description: Armored marine arthropods with compound eyes; one of the most successful animal groups, surviving almost 300 million years until the end-Permian extinction.
A Cambrian apex predator from the Burgess Shale: a stem-group arthropod with grasping frontal appendages and large compound eyes.
Five-eyed Burgess Shale animal with a long flexible proboscis ending in a grasping claw.
A small spiny worm on stilt-like legs, related to modern velvet worms; famously first reconstructed upside down.
An early chordate with a notochord and zig-zag muscle blocks, related to the ancestors of all vertebrates.
One of the earliest known vertebrates, from the Chengjiang biota of China: a tiny jawless fish with eyes and a skull of cartilage.
A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, among the largest animals of the Ordovician seas (maximum size is debated; often estimated at several metres).
One of the earliest vascular land plants: leafless, branching stems a few centimetres tall, tipped with spore capsules.

A single-celled freshwater predator about 50 micrometres across: a foamy, vacuolated sphere bristling with stiff radiating axopodia that snare passing flagellates and ciliates. Heliozoans leave no fossils, so it stands in for the ancient protist plankton that every later food web rests on.

A slipper-shaped ciliate about a quarter of a millimetre long, rowing through ponds on thousands of beating cilia and sweeping bacteria into its oral groove. Like most protists it leaves no fossils; it stands in for the ancient freshwater plankton.

A shapeless single cell that crawls by flowing into finger-like pseudopods and engulfs bacteria, algae and smaller protists whole. Soft-bodied amoebae leave almost no fossil record, so it stands in for the ancient protists of every age.

Not one animal but a colony of specialised zooids: a gas-filled float that sails on the wind, trailing stinging tentacles many metres long that paralyse fish. Siphonophores are soft-bodied and essentially absent from the fossil record; their cnidarian relatives go back to the Cambrian.

An egg-laying mammal from eastern Australia that hunts river invertebrates with eyes and ears shut, finding prey through electroreceptors in its rubbery bill. Males carry a venomous ankle spur. The living species is known from the Pleistocene; platypus relatives date back to the Cretaceous.

The bird with the longest wingspan alive, over three metres. It can glide for hours over the Southern Ocean without flapping, feeding on squid and fish, and returns to sub-Antarctic islands to raise a single chick every two years.

A bear from the mountain forests of central China that lives almost entirely on bamboo, eating for half the day and gripping stems with a thumb-like wrist bone. Its lineage reaches back into the Miocene; the living species appears in the Pleistocene.

Slender flies whose larvae filter-feed in still water while the adults sip nectar; only females take blood, to fuel their eggs. The oldest known mosquitoes are preserved in Cretaceous amber about 99 million years old.

One of the earliest trilobites, from the early and middle Cambrian of China and Australia: a spiny, crescent-headed scavenger and predator. Redlichia rex from South Australia grew to about 12 cm and had spiny legs for tearing up its food.

A large golden orb-weaver from East Asia, now spreading across the south-eastern United States. Females spin webs up to a metre across from golden silk; young spiders disperse by 'ballooning' on silk threads carried by the wind.

A sparrow-sized bird of Eurasian rivers and lakes that watches from a low perch, then plunges headfirst into the water after small fish. Its brilliant blue is structural colour, made by light scattering in the feathers rather than by pigment.

A long-legged shorebird of western North American wetlands that sweeps its upturned bill from side to side through shallow water to catch insects and crustaceans. Its head and neck turn cinnamon in the breeding season.

A ground-dwelling songbird of south-eastern Australian forests, famous for mimicry: displaying males copy other birds, and even chainsaws and camera shutters, while fanning a lacy silver tail over their heads.

The largest living marsupial, hopping across the Australian interior at up to 60 km/h on springy tendons that recycle energy with every bound. The joey is born the size of a bean and grows for months in its mother's pouch.
A heron-like bird of forest streams in Central and South America. Finely barred and well hidden at rest, it startles predators by spreading its wings into a display of two huge 'sunburst' eyespots.

A perching duck of wooded lakes and rivers in East Asia that nests in tree holes; the ducklings leap to the ground soon after hatching. The drake's upright orange 'sails' and whiskers make it one of the most ornate ducks in the world.

The most widespread large mammal of the Americas, from Canada to Peru. When alarmed it bounds away with its tail raised, flashing the white underside as a warning to the herd. Bucks regrow their antlers every year.

The only truly social cat: prides of related females hunt together while males defend the territory. Lions ranged across Africa, Eurasia and the Americas during the Pleistocene; today they survive in sub-Saharan Africa and India's Gir Forest.

A large, adaptable monkey of African savannas and woodland that lives in troops of up to 150 with complex social ranks. It eats almost anything, from grass and fruit to insects and the occasional small antelope.

A slow, gentle grazer of warm coasts and rivers from Florida to Brazil that can eat a tenth of its body weight in seagrass a day. Sea cows are distant relatives of elephants; their lineage goes back to the Eocene.
The longest member of the weasel family, up to 1.8 m, living in noisy family groups along Amazonian rivers. Each otter's creamy throat patch is unique, and families together will chase off caimans.

A gentle giant of tropical Indo-Pacific reefs, up to 5 m across, that filters plankton by gliding with its mouth wide open and its head fins unrolled. Mantas visit 'cleaning stations' where small fish pick parasites from their skin.

One of the heaviest bony fish, over two tonnes, shaped like a swimming head with tall fins and no real tail. It eats mostly jellyfish, basks on its side at the surface to warm up, and a female can carry 300 million eggs.
A small reef fish of the Indian and Pacific Oceans that feeds almost only on coral polyps, usually in faithful pairs. The black bar through its eye hides the real eye from predators.

A striking reef fish of the Indo-Pacific with bold black, white and yellow bands, a long snout for picking sponges from crevices, and a trailing white dorsal filament. It is the only living member of its family.

One of the largest flying animals ever, with a wingspan of about 10-11 metres and the standing height of a giraffe. It probably launched itself by vaulting on its folded wings and stalked small animals on foot like a giant stork. Late Cretaceous of North America.

One of the largest land predators ever, about 12 metres long and 8 tonnes, with the strongest bite of any known land animal, strong enough to crush bone. It lived in western North America at the very end of the Cretaceous, until the asteroid impact 66 million years ago.

Termites of northern Australia's tropical savannas that build earth mounds up to 8 metres tall, among the largest structures made by any animal besides humans. Soldiers defend the colony by squirting sticky glue from a pointed snout. Termites themselves date back to the Cretaceous.

A fast-growing Indo-Pacific reef coral that spreads into broad flat tables, shading the reef below. Like all reef-building corals it lives in partnership with photosynthetic algae in its tissues, which also give it its colour. Acropora corals appear in the fossil record in the Paleogene.

A slow-growing Caribbean coral whose boulder-shaped colonies are covered in maze-like grooves, each groove lined with polyps. Large heads can be several hundred years old and help build the backbone of the reef.

A branching Caribbean coral that grows in dense antler-like thickets, sheltering huge numbers of reef fish. Broken branches can regrow into new colonies. Once dominant on Caribbean reefs, it is now critically endangered.

A North American butterfly whose caterpillars feed on milkweed and store its toxins, so the bright orange adults are poisonous to birds. Each autumn millions migrate up to 4,000 km to overwinter in the mountain forests of Mexico.

The largest shark that ever lived, perhaps 15-20 metres long, with serrated teeth the size of a hand. It hunted whales in warm seas worldwide from about 23 to 3.6 million years ago. Only its teeth and a few vertebrae fossilise, so its body shape is reconstructed from relatives.

Europe's most familiar ladybird, which can eat thousands of aphids in its lifetime. Its red-and-black colours warn predators of bitter alkaloids it oozes from its leg joints when disturbed. Adults overwinter in clusters.

A brilliantly metallic leaf beetle of East Asia that feeds on dogbane and milkweed relatives, tolerating their toxic sap. Its shining blue-green colour comes from microscopic layers in the wing cases rather than pigment.

A large European earthworm that digs vertical burrows up to two metres deep and drags fallen leaves down into them at night. Its feeding and burrowing mix and aerate the soil; Darwin called earthworms some of the most important animals in history.

A large crocodilian of the swamps and rivers of the south-eastern United States, with a broad rounded snout. Females guard their nests and carry the hatchlings in their jaws. Its genus goes back over 30 million years to the Oligocene.

A large tree-dwelling lizard of Central and South American rainforests that eats leaves and fruit. It basks high in the canopy and, when threatened, drops into the water below and swims away. A light-sensing 'third eye' on top of its head helps it spot birds of prey.

A rattlesnake of the deserts of the south-western United States and north-west Mexico whose speckled colours match the local rock, from pale granite to dark lava. Heat-sensing pits on its face let it strike warm-blooded prey in the dark.

A large sea turtle of tropical and subtropical seas, named for the green fat that its diet of seagrass and algae gives it. Females swim thousands of kilometres back to the beaches where they hatched to lay their eggs. Sea turtles first appear in the Cretaceous.

A spiny grazer of the kelp forests of North America's Pacific coast that scrapes algae with a five-toothed jaw. Where sea otters, its main predator, disappear, urchin swarms can mow kelp forests down to bare 'urchin barrens'.

A bright red-orange encrusting sponge of Caribbean reefs and mangrove roots, studded with volcano-like vents that breathe out the water it has filtered. Its tissues carry toxins that cause a burning rash on human skin, which is how it got its name. Broken fragments can regrow into new sponges.

A half-millimetre, eight-legged micro-animal that lumbers through the water films of moss, lichen and pond sediment, piercing plant cells and tiny prey with its needle-like stylets. When its home dries out it curls into a dehydrated 'tun' and can survive freezing, boiling, crushing pressure, radiation and even the vacuum of space, reviving decades later when water returns.

Not a true eel but a South American knifefish up to two metres long. Most of its body is electric organ that can discharge over 600 volts to stun prey and deter predators, while weaker pulses let it sense its murky Amazon surroundings. It gulps air at the surface, taking most of its oxygen through its mouth.

A small bat of Central and South America that feeds only on blood, mostly from livestock and other large mammals. It lands near sleeping prey, runs and hops nimbly on its thumbs and hind legs, finds a warm spot with heat sensors on its nose, and laps blood from a tiny cut kept open by anticoagulant saliva. Roost-mates that failed to feed are given a shared meal of regurgitated blood.

One of the largest flying insects ever, with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres. This griffinfly, a relative of modern dragonflies, hunted other insects over the swampy coal forests of the Late Carboniferous, about 300 million years ago. Its size was possible partly because the air then held much more oxygen than today. It is known from fossils found at Commentry, France.

A social bee living in colonies of tens of thousands of workers around a single queen. Workers gather nectar and pollen from flowers, store honey in wax combs, and use the waggle dance to tell nestmates where food is. As pollinators of crops and wild plants, they are among the most important insects to people.

A squid-like belemnite that hunted with ten hooked arms in the shallow Sundance Sea of Wyoming about 160 million years ago. Its internal guard was the chunkiest of any belemnite, about 10 cm long but 6 cm wide, and it belonged to the megateuthidids, a family thought to have mostly died out millions of years earlier.

The 'star ammonite' of the Early Jurassic seas, about 195 million years ago. Its loosely coiled shell, up to 20 cm across, has bold straight ribs and a sharp keel flanked by two grooves. Gas-filled chambers kept it buoyant while the animal hunted small prey with its arms. Its fossils are so common at Lyme Regis that a whole rock zone is named after it.

Perhaps the strangest-looking ammonite, from the Late Cretaceous seas around Japan about 90 million years ago. After a few loose spiral whorls, its shell doubled back on itself in a chain of U-bends that wrap into a knot. The pattern looks random but follows a precise growth rule that kept the animal balanced, so it could drift through the water feeding on plankton.

North America's largest land bird, with a wingspan of nearly three metres. It soars for hours on thermals over canyons and hills looking for carcasses, and raises a single chick every year or two. In the Pleistocene it fed on mammoths and other large mammals. By 1987 only 27 were left, all taken into captivity, and a breeding programme has since returned hundreds to the wild.

A huge, warty toad from Central and South America, up to 15-24 cm long. The big glands behind its eyes ooze a milky poison strong enough to kill dogs, snakes and crocodiles, and a female can lay over 30,000 eggs at once. Released in Australia in 1935 to control cane beetles, it ignored the beetles and spread across the north of the continent, becoming one of the world's most notorious invasive species.
